Name: uav_night_small_objects
Title: How much of the day-to-night gap for small UAV objects does synthetic low-light training close?
Short Hypothesis: Fine-tuning a detector on daytime VisDrone images with physics-inspired synthetic low-light degradation closes a substantial fraction of the gap to training on real night images for small objects on held-out real night sequences, while test-time enhancement (gamma, CLAHE) helps small objects less than medium ones because it amplifies noise.
Related Work: VisDrone2019-DET (Zhu et al., TPAMI 2021) is a dense small-object UAV benchmark without illumination labels. MAET (Cui et al., ICCV 2021) synthesizes low-light training data with an unprocess/noise/ISP pipeline and evaluates COCO to ExDark, not UAV or object size. Lv et al. (IJCV 2021) simulate low light with noise. Zero-DCE++ (Li et al., TPAMI 2021) enhances without paired data. IA-YOLO (AAAI 2022), FeatEnHancer (ICCV 2023) and YOLA (NeurIPS 2024) learn illumination handling end to end; YOLA reports that several enhancers reduce detection AP on ExDark and notes that enhancement can impair small faces. PFNN (Frontiers in AI 2025) compared enhancers on an unpublished VisDrone night subset without size bins. Bridge (CVPR 2026) sets a day-to-dark protocol on DroneVehicle without augmentation baselines or size analysis. SAHI (ICIP 2022) and P2 heads improve VisDrone small objects but do not address illumination. To our knowledge no study measures synthetic-to-real low-light transfer by object size on UAV imagery; this is not a verified novelty claim.
Abstract: DATA: download VisDrone2019-DET train, val and test-dev zips from https://github.com/ultralytics/assets/releases/download/v0.0.0/ (VisDrone2019-DET-train.zip, VisDrone2019-DET-val.zip, VisDrone2019-DET-test-dev.zip) on the remote machine only. Prepare once per VM under /content/cache/visdrone: write a completion marker after every preparation step and reuse it, never re-download or re-derive; parallelize luminance measurement, conversion and degradation with a process pool of os.cpu_count() workers (a fresh single-process preparation took 19 minutes). Convert annotations to YOLO format like the Ultralytics VisDrone.yaml: drop class 0 (ignored regions) and class 11 (others), keep the 10 classes, clip boxes. PRE-REGISTERED ILLUMINATION GROUPS: per-image median luma of the grayscale image resized to a 256 px long side, in [0,1]. day: median >= 0.30; night: median < 0.16; twilight: in between (a pilot found 3950/597/520 day-train/tune/test and 1278 night images, visually confirmed as night scenes). Sequence id = the first underscore-separated filename field. Splits (seed 0, all by sequence id so no sequence crosses splits): day-train/day-tune = 90/10 of train-split day images; day-test = val-split day images; night images pooled from train, val and test-dev are split 40/60 by sequence into night-train and night-test; twilight-test = twilight images from val and test-dev. Print and save group counts, sequence counts and a montage of 24 random night-test images. night-test must never be used for training, tuning, early stopping or model selection. TRAINING ARMS (identical model, epochs, batch, optimizer, schedule, Ultralytics augmentation and number of training images; only the images differ): A = day-train unchanged; B = day-train where a seeded random 50% of images are replaced by synthetic low-light copies; C (real-night reference, an upper bound, not a proposed method) = day-train where randomly chosen day images are replaced by all night-train images, keeping the count equal to A. Report gap closure = (B - A) / (C - A) on night-test per seed and area bin, and only interpret it when C - A is clearly larger than seed variation. SYNTHETIC LOW LIGHT: convert sRGB to linear (gamma 2.2), multiply by exposure k ~ LogUniform(0.05, 0.3), add Poisson-Gaussian noise in linear space with shot variance a*x, a ~ LogUniform(1e-4, 1e-2) and read-noise std s ~ LogUniform(1e-3, 1e-2), clip, re-apply gamma 1/2.2, quantize to uint8 JPEG quality 95. Arm B copies depend on the training seed; synthetic-dark versions of day-tune and day-test use fixed seed 12345. DETECTOR: Ultralytics YOLO11s fine-tuned from COCO-pretrained yolo11s.pt (fall back to yolov8s.pt only if yolo11s is unavailable, and record which). Stage 2 chooses imgsz from {640, 960, 1280} and the epoch count; then every arm uses those settings. Pass device=0 to train/val/predict and never call .to(device) on a YOLO object before training: in Ultralytics 8.4 that raises 'Expected all tensors to be on the same device' in _remap_cls_by_names. Use cache='ram' when the VM has enough memory, else 'disk', workers=os.cpu_count(), verbose=False, plots=False, and write Ultralytics run directories under /content/cache/runs, not the job workspace; copy only small result files back. TEST-TIME ENHANCEMENT on night-test and twilight-test for arms A, B and C: none; gamma with exponent mapping the image median luma to 0.35 (exponent clipped to [0.3, 1]); CLAHE on the LAB L channel (clipLimit 2.0, tile 8x8). EVALUATION: inference at the training imgsz, conf 0.001, max_det 1000, predictions mapped to original resolution, pycocotools COCOeval against COCO JSON ground truth at original resolution. Report AP, AP50 and AP per area bin at original resolution: tiny (<16^2), small (16^2 to 32^2), small_all (<32^2, the primary endpoint), medium (32^2 to 96^2), large; for day-tune, synthetic-dark-tune, day-test, synthetic-dark-test, night-test and twilight-test. Selection metric for choosing configurations: mean AP on day-tune and synthetic-dark-tune only; label night-test metrics report_only. COMPUTE: the study may use most of a ~185 compute-unit budget; an A100 costs about 5.4 units/hour. Declare A100 for full-schedule training, L4 or T4 for short pilots. Wall-clock targets per script: stage 1 (short schedule, a few epochs) 30 minutes; stage 2 (arm A only) 60 minutes; stage 3 (arms A, B, C) 2 hours; stage 4 (only arm B and its ablated variants, at the stage-3 schedule) 90 minutes; the hard limit is 2.5 hours. Exceeding the budget stops the whole study, so keep within these targets. Measure seconds per epoch and choose epochs to fit. Read the training seed from os.environ.get('AUTORESEARCH_SEED', '0') and keep data splits and synthetic test degradations fixed across seeds. Print the GPU name, torch and ultralytics versions (as str), epoch time and total runtime. Save every metric, count, setting, seed and version in experiment_data.npy (under 5 MB; at most 8 small uint8 example images) and never fabricate or estimate a metric that was not computed. Plotting and metric parsing run locally without torch or a GPU: use only numpy, matplotlib and the standard library. Absolute AP is not comparable to published VisDrone results, which use 300 or more epochs.
Experiments: Stage 1: implement data preparation, illumination and sequence splits, COCO evaluation and arms A, B and C with a short schedule on a cheap GPU; verify counts, the night montage and finite metrics.
Stage 2: tune only the shared schedule for arm A (imgsz 640/960/1280, epochs, learning rate, batch) by the selection metric within the time limit; every arm then uses these settings.

Stage 3: main comparison of arms A, B and C at the full schedule with test-time none/gamma/CLAHE, three seeds, paired per-seed differences and gap closure in small_all AP on night-test, and the day-test guard (no drop above 1 AP).

Stage 4 ablations of arm B (train arm B and the ablated variants only): darkening without noise, noise only at normal exposure, replacement fraction 0.25 and 0.75, and a warm colour cast typical of sodium street lights; report which component carries any real-night gain.
Report negative and null results; state effect sizes against seed variability rather than significance.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Night is defined by a luminance threshold, not by capture metadata; misassigned dusk or shaded images can bias night groups.
Night images come from a limited number of sequences, so sequence-level variation dominates; night-test scenes may share locations with daytime training scenes.
Arm C uses real night images and is a reference, not a method; its gap estimate depends on the night-train sequences.
Fine-tuning schedules are short relative to published work, so absolute AP is not comparable.
Ignored regions are dropped, so detections inside them count as false positives equally in every arm.
Three training seeds do not capture dataset variability; conclusions are limited to VisDrone and one detector family.
Synthetic degradation gains alone do not support the hypothesis; only real night-test results do.
